entries.title: About the Course
entries.content:
Students spend a term learning the structure of our local and state governments, then turn to key primary source documents related to our government before ending the year with an introduction to economics, focusing on the history of money, the banking system, and personal finance.

This topic is included in the following course(s): Citizenship: Grade 8 (U.S.)

entries.title: Placement & Combining Tips
entries.content: If a student hasn't studied the Constitution, consider having them take the 7th-grade government course first.

blocks.text:
Plutarch: Teachers will find it helpful to preread the entire Life first, and then preread the day’s passage before each lesson. Mark any passages that should be omitted due to content. (In Anne White’s Plutarch Project books, the recommended source for this course, objectionable content has already been omitted.)

Current Events: Preview the news source for suitability.

Most other citizenship topics don't require additional prep.
Connect back to the previous lesson. (Optional for Current Events).

For news sources, show students how to scan the headlines to get an overview first and then choose a story to read. 

For Plutarch or other books: Use a picture, a map, or an engaging question to prepare students to receive the story as relevant. You may talk about one or two unfamiliar words that will be crucial to understanding. It is not necessary to cover all unfamiliar words.

Read the selection assigned or the news story chosen. For rich, dense, or more challenging books such as Ourselves and Plutarch, it is a good idea to read them aloud. Have students keep an eye out for things to add to their Citizenship Notebook, Book of Centuries, and/or Commonplace book.
Have the students narrate orally or in writing.

Give students an opportunity to share their thoughts on the story and any connections made. For current events, look up where events occurred on a map and ask questions to help students discern the quality of the piece. (e.g., Are there sources cited? Is there an obvious bias? If so, what do other authors have to say on this subject? Are arguments supported by evidence? Is that evidence credible?) Consider reading an alternative perspective.
Have students record important ideas in their Citizenship Notebooks.

lessons.title: 30m American Gov./ Economics: Grade 8 - Lesson 2

Origins of Authority: Constitutions & Police Powers
⍞ Materials: Reading PDF

➜ INTRO
States have two sources of authority that allow them to create and enforce laws: 1) constitutional powers and 2) police powers. These sources of authority are the basis for the laws and regulations that states pass, as well as the authority that states grant to smaller local governments, like cities and towns. 

➜ READ

lessons.title: 30m American Gov./ Economics: Grade 8 - Lesson 13
lessons.body:
A Young Nation: American Government from 1800 to 1900
⍞ Materials: Reading PDF Part 1

➜ INTRO
Welcome back to American Government! Last year, you learned about the formation of the American Government and the reasoning behind why the Constitution and Bill of Rights were drafted and negotiated as they were. This year, we move forward to the period from 1800 to 1900 and study how the new government began to take action and shape the first hundred years of our country’s history. 

➜ READ
∞ Link: Reading PDF Part 1
Week 1 

• With any time that you have remaining, read your summary statements and skim any written narrations from the last two years of American Government. Your summary statements should cover the time periods from Rotation 1 (800-1650 AD) and Rotation 2 (1650-1800 AD). 

➜ REFLECT
Talk about the summary statements you have reviewed with your teacher or classmates. What did you remember? What had you forgotten? Did anything come to mind as you were reviewing that you had not thought about before?
lessons.teacherNotes:
★ TEACHER NOTE
One week is built in at the end of this term for “catch-up” reading, in case you miss a week or a reading takes you longer than your allotted time to complete. Please do not skip ahead if you have not completed the lesson from the week before – work through the weeks chronologically and use the catch-up week (Week 11) as necessary.  

Optional Activity: Guide students in creating a bulleted list of keywords that they notice while reading their summary statements or during their discussion. Keywords can be words that were repeated frequently, or that stood out to the student for any particular reason (there is no “right” set of keywords). This activity is optional because it requires students to exercise a higher-level analysis and might not be a useful reflective tool for all students.

lessons.title: 30m American Gov./ Economics: Grade 8 - Lesson 14
lessons.body:
Western Expansion and the Missouri Compromise (1820)
⍞ Materials: Reading PDF Part 1

➜ INTRO
The United States nearly doubled in size following the purchase of the Louisiana Territory from France. As new states began to petition Congress for entry to the country, the issue of slavery began to divide the nation. In 1820, Congress passed the Missouri Compromise, defining geographical boundaries that would determine whether slavery would be legal in new states. The Compromise would be followed by a series of legislative acts that together attempted to bind the new country together in the face of rapid land expansion and deep divides over slavery. 

➜ READ
∞ Link: Reading PDF Part 1
Week 2

➜ REFLECT
Narrate. Write a summary statement or short narration describing the main ideas from this week’s reading.

lessons.title: 30m American Gov./ Economics: Grade 8 - Lesson 15
lessons.body:
Western Expansion and the Compromise of 1850
⍞ Materials: Reading PDF Part 1

➜ INTRO
Although the Missouri Compromise remained in effect, the acquisition of the western territory from Texas to modern-day California following the Mexican-American War reignited the question of whether new states formed from this territory would be admitted as slave states or free states. In order to maintain a tentative balance of slave to free states across the nation, Congress passed the Compromise of 1850 after efforts to ban slavery entirely from the new territory failed. 

➜ READ
∞ Link: Reading PDF Part 1
Week 3

➜ REFLECT
Narrate. Write a summary statement or short narration describing the main ideas from this week’s reading.

lessons.title: 30m American Gov./ Economics: Grade 8 - Lesson 16
lessons.body:
Western Expansion and the Kansas-Nebraska Act
⍞ Materials: Reading PDF Part 1

➜ INTRO
The Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854 repealed the Missouri Compromise in its entirety and allowed the new territories of Kansas and Nebraska to decide the question of whether slavery would be allowed in the territories by popular sovereignty – by a vote of the people of the territories. Violence stemming from pro-slavery and abolitionist clashes in Kansas and in Washington, D.C., earned the nickname “Bleeding Kansas” and foreshadowed the start of the Civil War. 

➜ READ
∞ Link: Reading PDF Part 1
Week 4

➜ REFLECT
Consider the three major pieces of Congressional legislation that you have studied over the last three weeks: the Missouri Compromise, the Compromise of 1850, and the Kansas-Nebraska Act. Why do you think that Representatives and Senators in Congress increasingly decided to turn the slavery question over to popular vote? What benefits are there to a popular vote? What drawbacks or dangers might there be to a popular vote? 

• Write a summary statement or short narration explaining your thoughts in response to these questions.

lessons.title: 30m American Gov./ Economics: Grade 8 - Lesson 17
lessons.body:
Treaties and the Removal of Tribal Nations (Part I)
⍞ Materials: Reading PDF Part 1

➜ INTRO
Treaties are a tool that the Constitution allows the President to use in order to make formal agreements between the United States and another nation. Over the first four decades of the 19th century, the United States began to engage in treaty-making with American Indian Tribes, located in what are now the southern states of Tennessee, Alabama, Georgia, Florida, and Mississippi, with the goal of removing these Tribes from the South and relocating them west of the Mississippi River. 

➜ READ
∞ Link: Reading PDF Part 1
Week 5

➜ REFLECT
Narrate. Write a summary statement or short narration describing the main ideas from this week’s reading.

lessons.title: 30m American Gov./ Economics: Grade 8 - Lesson 18
lessons.body:
Treaties and the Removal of Tribal Nations (Part II)
⍞ Materials: Reading PDF Part 1

➜ INTRO
With the Indian Removal Act of 1830, Congress indicated its support for the removal of tribes, specifically authorizing then-President Andrew Jackson to use treaties to effect land exchanges, trading land west of the Mississippi to tribes in exchange for tribal land in the South. But was the Indian Removal Act constitutional, and were the treaties themselves enforceable? We will explore the Act and its impact further in this week’s reading.  

➜ READ
∞ Link: Reading PDF Part 1
Week 6

➜ REFLECT
Narrate. Write a summary statement or short narration describing the main ideas from this week’s reading.

lessons.title: 30m American Gov./ Economics: Grade 8 - Lesson 19
lessons.body:
Tribal Nations before the Supreme Court
⍞ Materials: Reading PDF Part 2

➜ INTRO
While President Jackson and Congress worked to remove Tribes from the South by means of treaties and federal legislation, the Cherokee Nation sought to enforce its treaty rights before the Supreme Court. Over the course of two decisions within the span of the same number of years, the Supreme Court set precedent that would define the rights and status of Tribes into the modern day, and by extension, undermined the integrity of the federal government’s treaty-making with these Tribes. The Indian Appropriations Act, passed in 1871 by Congress, would end treaty-making with Tribes altogether. 

➜ READ
∞ Link: Reading PDF Part 2
Week 7

➜ REFLECT
Narrate. Write a summary statement or short narration describing the main ideas from this week’s reading.

lessons.title: 30m American Gov./ Economics: Grade 8 - Lesson 20
lessons.body:
Congress & Southern Secession
⍞ Materials: Reading PDF Part 2

➜ INTRO
On December 20, 1860, South Carolina seceded from the United States. Over the next seven months, ten more states would follow suit. Four of these states drafted formal Declarations of Causes that set forth their justifications for secession. This week, we will explore these Declarations in more detail and consider the impact that southern secession had on the federal Congress the states left behind.

➜ READ
∞ Link: Reading PDF Part 2
Week 8

➜ REFLECT
Consider how the various southern secession documents compare or contrast with the Declaration of Independence. What strikes you as similar or different? Among other things, you want to think about the organization or length of the documents, the reasons given for separation, and the historical events occurring at the time that each document was signed. 

• Write a summary statement or short narration describing the main ideas from this week’s reading.
lessons.teacherNotes:
★ TEACHER NOTE
If you have a group of students, pose this question for group discussion as an alternative to traditional narration. If you are the only student in your class, jot down some of the similarities or differences that you think of.

lessons.title: 30m American Gov./ Economics: Grade 8 - Lesson 21
lessons.body:
Congress & the Reconstruction Acts
⍞ Materials: Reading PDF Part 2

➜ INTRO
Following the end of the Civil War and preliminary reconstruction efforts by President Johnson, Congress exerted control over the Reconstruction project by passing a series of acts now known as the Reconstruction Acts. These Acts, passed over a presidential veto by Johnson, established military control in southern states that had seceded and established strict standards for readmission to the Union. 

➜ READ
∞ Link: Reading PDF Part 2
Week 9

➜ REFLECT
Narrate. Write a summary statement or short narration describing the main ideas from this week’s reading.

lessons.title: 30m American Gov./ Economics: Grade 8 - Lesson 22
lessons.body:
“Defective from the Start”: The Constitution, Slavery, & the Civil War Amendments
⍞ Materials: Reading PDF Part 2

➜ INTRO
In addition to taking control of Reconstruction following the close of the Civil War, Congress also proposed three amendments to the Constitution. These amendments, now known as the Civil War Amendments, banned slavery and established a series of protections and rights that are now foundational to how we think about citizenship in the United States. It would be five years before these amendments were fully ratified by the states, and it would be nearly a hundred more years until the Civil Rights Movement would take up the vision for justice and equality that these amendments had begun to advance.

➜ READ
∞ Link: Reading PDF Parţ 2
Week 10

➜ REFLECT
Narrate. Write a summary statement or short narration describing the main ideas from this week’s reading.

lessons.title: 30m American Gov./ Economics: Grade 8 - Lesson 25
lessons.body:
⍞ Materials: Dollars & Sense, Citizenship notebook

➜ INTRO
Are you familiar with the Bible verse, "The love of money is a root of all kinds of evil" (I Timothy 6:10)?  What do you think that means, and how have you seen that truth play out? This term, we will be studying economics, which has to do with money and the way a country uses and produces goods and services.

➜ READ, NARRATE, & DISCUSS
1\. Introduction ix-xiii "Bread. Dough." - "dollars and cents." 
2\. p.8 "You've Got It and I Want It: The Law of Supply and Demand"

• How does money help the economy, and how does greed hurt the economy?

➜ VIEW & DISCUSS        
∞ Video Link: What is Supply and Demand?

• Explain the economic principle "The Law of Supply and Demand."

➜ CITIZENSHIP NOTEBOOK (Make a section in your notebook or binder called Economics)
1\. Make a list of the goods and services your family uses that contribute toward a healthy economy. Goods are tangible things you buy, such as clothes and food. Services are intangible and usually involve paying for a business to do something for you. Examples: haircuts, car insurance, phone service.
2\. Can you think of examples that fit the economic principle of the Law of Supply and Demand? Also, make a list of items that may be in high demand or low demand depending on the time of year.

terms.content: · Reading PDF: Describe your state government as it is created by your state constitution. Include 1) what the different branches are, 2) the powers that the different branches have, and 3) if your constitution had a preamble, what problems or goals the preamble tried to address. OR Describe the differences between the federal government, your state government, and your local government.

· Reading PDF: Tell about the expansion of the United States into the southeast and the relocation of Tribal Nations. What actions did Congress, the President, and/or the Supreme Court take with regard to Removal? How did tribes respond to Removal efforts? 
                                                 OR 
Tell about the Southern secession and the actions that Congress took in response to the outbreak of the Civil War and as part of Reconstruction following the Civil War. Bonus: How many branches of government became involved in the reconstruction work, and what role did those branches play?
· Dollars & Sense: Tell what you know about the formation of the national banking system OR Tell what you know about the services banks offer.
